note: Generated from the pitchunfairly.com templates (unfairly-app apps/decks/src/arcade). Do not edit by hand.

categories.name: Pitch decks
categories.useWhen: Raising money from investors, from pre-seed to growth rounds.
categories.length: Pre-seed 8 to 12, seed 12 to 15, Series A 15 to 20, growth 18 to 25 plus a data appendix.
categories.format: Sent first, then presented. It must make sense without the founder in the room.
rules: Investors skim: DocSend measured about 3.7 minutes per deck, and decks that fail are dropped in about 2. The first two slides decide whether the rest gets read.
Every headline is a full-sentence claim, and each beat gets one slide, three at most (Y Combinator).
Lead with your strongest proof, traction or team, whichever is stronger.
Size the market bottoms-up (customers × price), with the math visible.
The ask names an amount, the milestone it buys, and when.
failures: A top-down TAM with no path to it
Traction buried after the product tour

categories.name: Sales
categories.useWhen: Winning a deal: first calls, champion decks forwarded internally, business cases, customer reviews.
categories.length: First call 3 to 5 plus discovery questions; narrative 8 to 12; champion deck 8 to 10.
categories.format: Presented in conversation; champion decks are sent and must stand alone.
rules: Open on a big shift in the buyer's world, not on your company (Raskin's strategic narrative).
On discovery calls, slides cost follow-ups: Gong found reps who used them were 17% less likely to book the next meeting. Ask, then show.
Winners spend less time on the deck (9.1 vs 11.4 minutes in intro calls) and 39% less on features (Gong).
Use proof from customers like the buyer; generic logos and ROI claims hurt (Gong).
End on a mutual action plan with dates and owners on both sides, never "Thank you".
failures: No next step with a date

categories.name: Board and investor updates
categories.useWhen: Board meetings, monthly or quarterly investor updates, crisis plans.
categories.length: Board deck 10 to 12 plus appendix; investor update one screen to 8 slides.
categories.format: A pre-read sent 1 to 7 days ahead; the meeting is for discussion and decisions.
rules: Open with a TL;DR and the asks; investors and boards read the top first.
Score last period's priorities red, yellow, or green before anything new.
Every metric against plan and against trend, never alone.
Lowlights before highlights; the board finds them anyway.
Close on the decisions you need from the board, then next period's priorities with one owner each. Detail goes in the appendix.
failures: A product demo instead of a review
No decision asked of the board

categories.name: Everyday work
categories.useWhen: Project status updates, executive briefings, roadmaps and the other recurring decks a team reads every week.
categories.length: Status update one screen to 6 slides; briefing 1 to 3 plus appendix; roadmap 5 to 8.
categories.format: Mostly read, not presented. Each slide has to work without a speaker.
rules: Answer first: lead with the conclusion, then the evidence (Minto). In a controlled study, sentence headlines with visual evidence beat topic titles with bullets on comprehension (Garner, Alley et al. 2013).
Status has fixed meanings: green is on track, amber means a risk with a fix in hand, red means we need help (Atlassian).
Show progress as movement since last time, not a list of activity.
Every risk has an owner and a date; every ask names who must decide.
Roadmaps show confidence by horizon (Now, Next, Later), with dates only where they are real.
failures: Everything green until it is suddenly red
The conclusion on the last slide
A roadmap of promised dates nobody believes

categories.name: Launches and keynotes
categories.useWhen: Launching a product or campaign, keynotes, big internal or external reveals.
categories.format: Presented live, with a demo; shared afterwards as a link.
rules: Name the moment: why this matters today.
Show what is broken about today's options before the reveal.
One reveal, then no more than three things it does.
Demo moments over feature lists; each slide shows one thing working.
Close on price, availability, and a date.

categories.name: Proposals and business cases
categories.useWhen: Client proposals, RFP responses, budget requests, internal business cases.
categories.format: Sent to be read and compared, then presented to decide.
rules: Start with their goal in their words, not your company.
Check off every requirement in the brief, visibly.
Put the decision on the first slide: what you are asking them to approve.
Show the options you considered and why this one wins.
Cost, phasing, and terms in one place; risks each with an owner; next steps with a date.
failures: A credentials deck instead of an answer
Missing a requirement from the brief

categories.name: Team and culture
categories.useWhen: All-hands and policy announcements, culture decks, recruiting and hiring pitches.
categories.length: All-hands 10 to 12; culture 12 to 20; recruiting 10 to 11.
categories.format: Presented to the team, then sent; recruiting decks are sent to candidates.
rules: All-hands: what happened, the number that matters, the decision, what changes for you, why, what is not changing, an FAQ, what is next.
Say what changes for each person before why it is good for the company.
Culture decks describe behaviors, not words: who you hire, promote, and let go for.
Recruiting decks put the hard parts up front; the right people self-select.
failures: Selling a job without its hard parts

categories.name: Reviews and post-mortems
categories.useWhen: Incident reviews, project post-mortems, retros, case studies.
categories.format: Sent as a written record; presented to decide on action items.
rules: Blameless: systems and decisions, not people.
Summary and impact first, then a timeline logged to the minute.
Separate detection, response, and root cause; ask why five times.
Name what went well, what went wrong, and where you got lucky.
Every action item has an owner and a date.
failures: A root cause that stops at the first why

categories.name: Strategy and planning
categories.useWhen: Annual plans, strategy offsites, OKRs, big bets.
categories.format: A pre-read for leadership, then presented to align.
rules: Score last year before planning the next.
Name the few bets and, just as clearly, what you will stop doing.
Targets with owners and dates; resources follow the bets.

categories.name: Just for fun
categories.useWhen: Party pitches, persuading friends or family, celebrations.
categories.format: Presented live to a room that is in on the joke.
rules: Use a serious business format for personal stakes; the deadpan is the joke.
Real details beat generic ones: names, prices, dates.
End with a vote or an ask the room can answer on the spot.
failures: Jokes that need the format explained

templates.name: Airbnb: Seed deck
templates.hook: Air mattresses to $2.1B of math.
whatMakesItWork: The market math is live: Drag your share of trips and watch the circle and the revenue recalculate. The pitch is the formula.
The product plays itself: Search, listing, booked: the three-step flow animates on a phone instead of sitting in three screenshots.
One receipt replaces three bullets: The problem slide is a hotel bill: $282, locals met 0, real city seen 0.
Press and testimonials cut: Fourteen slides became ten. Investors skim for about three minutes, so the low-weight slides went.

beats.job: Say the product in a sentence a friend could repeat.
Make the pain concrete: a price, a moment, a receipt.
Show who wins, one card per side of the market.
Point at people already doing it the hard way.
Bottoms-up: trips × share × fee, with the math visible.
Show the flow in three steps.
Name the channels you will actually use.
A 2×2 where you are alone in the corner that matters.
Why these people, in one line each.
An amount tied to one milestone and a date.

templates.name: Uber: UberCab concept deck
templates.hook: Push a button, get a car. In 2008.
whatMakesItWork: The product drives itself: Press "Request UberCab" and a car drives the streets of SF to your pin while the ETA counts down from 5. The original described it in bullets.
The market slide has a twist: The 2008 headline stays $4.2B. Then drag "what if hailing becomes a habit" toward the dashed square: $65B of 2019 gross bookings.
One dispatch call replaces a bullet list: "Cabs in 2008" is a call screen counting to 45 minutes: radio dispatch, no GPS, no ETA, cash.
Twenty-five slides became eleven: Use cases, benefits, marketing ideas, and the LBS roadmap folded into the beats that carry the story.

beats.job: Say the whole product in four words and show the button.
Put the audience in the old experience: the call, the wait, the cash.
One ratio that shows why incumbents won't fix it.
The technology shift that just made the idea possible.
An analogy investors already understand: the NetJets of X.
Play the core action, start to finish.
How you will run it, ending on the business model.
One concrete edge, charted: here, the fleet.
The number, who holds it, and how it grows.
Worst, realistic, best: show the floor is fine.
What is done, and the next milestone with a date.

templates.name: Snapchat: Series A deck
templates.hook: Ten seconds, then gone. Facebook wanted it anyway.
whatMakesItWork: The demo is a real snap: Tap to open it, watch ten seconds run out, and it is gone. You can send another, but you cannot get that one back.
The growth chart scrubs: Drag from launch day to the pitch and watch snaps a day climb from about 2 million to 60 million, with Facebook's copy marked on the way.
The skeptics get a slide: The class that called it a bad idea and the press that called it a sexting app sit next to the teenager who already knew.
It ends on the no: A kicker slide jumps nine months ahead: 400 million snaps a day and a reported $3 billion offer, opened and declined.

beats.job: Show the product's one rule in a sentence and a picture.
Name the pressure everyone feels and nobody says out loud.
The counterintuitive bet, set side by side with the old way.
Let the room use the product for ten seconds.
Put the skeptics on the slide, then the user who proves them wrong.
One usage number, plotted over time, with the milestones marked.
Prove the habit: daily use, opens a day, retention.
Show the biggest player copying you, and what happened next.
Explain why this is a new behavior and not a feature.
How few people are carrying how much load.
The amount, the lead, and the two things the money buys.
Leave them with the stakes: what this is worth if it works.

templates.name: LinkedIn: Series B deck
templates.hook: Promised. Delivered. Repeat.
whatMakesItWork: Promised flips to delivered: Four Series A promises sit on cards that turn over to the result with a stamp: about 400K members promised, 930K+ delivered.
The tagline becomes a graph: "Your network is bigger than you think" grows ring by ring, counting each degree, and a toggle adds Network Plus's fourth.
Three revenue streams light up: Ads, listings, and subscriptions light one by one over the free network. Tap one to isolate its price and launch date.
Thesis first, thesis last: Reid's own advice, applied: the thesis moves from slide 36 to slide 2, and the close merges the ask with the cover line.

beats.job: The thesis as one sentence a stranger could repeat.
What investors must believe, in three lines.
Answer the scariest question (no revenue) before the product.
Name how it is done today and why each way fails.
Line up winners investors already understand, ending on you.
Show the mechanism that makes it big, not a claim.
One precedent that proves the order of operations.
Last round's promises next to the results.
Your share of the category, with the field named.
Projections conservative enough to pass the blink test.
Who executes, and who already bet on them.
The amount, what it unlocks, and the thesis left on screen.

templates.name: Scrub Daddy: The Shark Tank pitch
templates.modelName: Scrub Daddy's Shark Tank pitch structure (ask, demo, numbers, objections, deal)
templates.hook: A smiley sponge, a $1M ask, and the deal the show is known for.
whatMakesItWork: The valuation math is live: Drag the cash and the equity and watch the implied valuation, the multiple of sales and five Shark fins react. Price it rich and the fins sink.
The demo has a tap: Turn the water from cold to warm and the sponge goes from firm to soft on screen, the way it did on the show.
The grill fits on one slide: Sales, cost to make, wholesale price, margin, channel and use of funds: the six questions every Shark asks, answered before they ask.
The bidding plays offer by offer: Step through the ask, the opening bid, the royalty and the final offer, each priced on the same line, until the deal stamp lands.

beats.job: Say the amount and the equity in the first breath. The valuation is the first thing they compute.
Show cash divided by equity, before and after the money, and the multiple of sales it implies.
A pain every investor has felt personally, shown in one picture.
One gesture that makes the product obvious. If it can be touched, let them touch it.
The founder story that explains why you, specifically, found this.
Sell-through, not interest: units per store, per day, against the alternative.
Sales, cost to make, price, margin, how you find customers, and what the money is for. One slide.
The four doubts they are about to raise, each answered in a line with a fact.
Every offer on the same line: cash, equity, implied valuation. Know your walk-away number.
Pick the investor who moves your hardest number, and say why.
Say the deal out loud, then the result it should lead to.

templates.name: The Wolf of Wall Street: Sell me this pen
templates.modelName: the sell me this pen discovery call structure (ask, create the need, then show)
templates.hook: Hand them a napkin before you hand them a pen.
whatMakesItWork: Run the napkin yourself: Four beats, clickable or on autoplay: ask for a signature, hear "I don't have a pen", hand it over, watch the signature draw on.
Watch the room react: Toggle the same five people between "describe the pen" and "create the need" and watch the interest meter and their faces change.
Questions before the pen: Five discovery questions on an order ticket, each with what it finds, so the pen stays in your pocket for eighteen minutes.
It ends on a calendar invite: A mutual action plan with owners on both sides and an accepted follow-up. The pen stays with the buyer.

beats.job: The outcome for the buyer, with the product held back on purpose.
Tell them they will do most of the talking, and when the product comes out.
Name the pitch they have heard a hundred times, so you can skip it.
Five questions: how often, where, the last bad time, who else suffers, what it cost.
A small, real moment where the buyer needs the thing before you show it.
The buyer states the problem. Write it down and play it back in their language.
Their numbers from discovery, showing how big and how urgent it is.
One slide, three promises, each tied to something they said.
Side by side: the same buyer with and without it, or a customer like them who said yes.
Answer each one with a question that sends them back to the need.
The structure on one page, so a champion can retell it.
A dated follow-up with owners on both sides, booked before you hang up.

templates.name: Netflix: Culture deck
templates.hook: 125 slides that rewired Silicon Valley.
whatMakesItWork: The Keeper Test is a game: Pick a teammate from a "Who's on your team?" profile screen and get the deck's own verdict, from Keep to a generous severance.
Context and control, one toggle: The same org flips between a boss approving every call and a team running on shared context. It plays control first, then lands on context.
The vacation policy deletes itself: Four lines of typical HR policy backspace away until one sentence is left: there is no policy or tracking.
125 slides became 11: Every one of the seven aspects survives, one idea per screen, dressed as a streaming title instead of a wall of text.

beats.job: Name the culture in two words people will repeat.
Define values by who gets hired, promoted, and let go, not by the lobby poster.
List the few behaviors you actually hire and fire on, one line each.
Give managers one test they can run on anyone today.
Say the line most culture decks won't, in full screen.
Show what happens to rules when talent density falls, and your answer.
Kill one real policy on stage to show you mean it.
Contrast the managing style you reject with the one you expect.
Agree on the what, free the how.
Tie pay to the value of the best people, with the math.
Close on the promise and what comes next.

templates.name: Christopher Columbus: The Atlantic seed round
templates.hook: Asia is just west. Probably.
whatMakesItWork: The math is a slider: Drag the Earth from Columbus's 75% to its real size and watch Japan slide off to 10,600 miles, uncovering a continent nobody budgeted for.
The roadmap sails itself: Seventy days, Palos to the Bahamas, drawn day by day with a counter and the real log: the second logbook, the birds, the near mutiny.
The cap table flips: Who pays (the Crown, a borrowed eighth, and a town paying off a fine) turns into who gets paid: 90% and 10%, tax free, forever.
A risk slide that misses one: Edge of the world, crew morale, Portugal, the committee: all handled. A continent in the way: not considered.

beats.job: Say the whole plan in five words.
Show the toll everyone already pays, stop by stop.
One picture of the shortcut.
The event that just freed the buyer's budget.
Size it with the best source in the room.
Put the key estimate on a slider and let them check it.
Be honest about the number; sell the persistence.
One line each, and why this crew will sign on.
A map of their long way round and your straight line.
Dated milestones you can scrub through.
Name every objection before the room does.
Who pays, who gets paid, and the titles on the door.

templates.name: The Trojan Horse: Trojan Horse launch
templates.modelName: the Trojan Horse product launch structure
templates.hook: A gift they can't refuse.
whatMakesItWork: The capacity fills up: A black-figure cross-section of the horse boards thirty soldiers, seat by seat, as the count climbs to "At capacity".
Trust is a live metric: Click through the gift, the retreat, Sinon, Laocoön and the serpents and watch Troy's trust climb, dip, and max out.
Launch night counts down: A clock runs to nightfall, the sky goes from ochre to moonlight, and the gates swing open from the inside.
The risk register is real: Laocoön, Cassandra, and Helen doing your wives' voices: every risk happened, every mitigation worked, all straight from Virgil and Homer.

beats.job: Name the product and the outcome in five words.
One brutal scoreboard: how long you have tried, and the zero.
The reframe: what the buyer refuses, next to what they welcome.
Specs and capacity, shown filling up.
The route, drawn on a map, including the part nobody sees.
The story the market will repeat, written as the release.
What the buyer reads on the label versus what it is.
One metric across the story beats, dips included.
A register with an owner and a mitigation for each.
A countdown to the moment it goes live.
Three line items and the return.

templates.name: Alexander Hamilton: National bank pitch
templates.modelName: Hamilton's 1790 Report on Public Credit structure
templates.hook: A broke country, one dinner, and a credit score.
whatMakesItWork: Thirteen debts roll into one: A live dashboard rolls every state’s debt into one federal number. Click Massachusetts out and watch the total drop.
The speculator math, on a slider: Drag what a veteran sold his $1,000 certificate for, then flip between Hamilton’s plan and Madison’s. 6.7x is why Madison was furious.
The dinner deal plays out: Two chits cross Jefferson’s table: the capital on the Potomac one way, votes for assumption the other, and a gold seal lands on it.
40,000 words, twelve slides: A Treasury report the length of a novella becomes a Series A(ssumption) deck with traction, a team, and reluctant board observers.

beats.job: The whole plan in four words: pay the debt, buy the trust.
One artifact that shows the pain: a $100 certificate that sold for $10.
The idea that makes the plan obvious, drawn as a loop.
Four moves, each with a date, one in focus.
Let the audience build the total themselves.
Model the critic’s case honestly, then show the vote.
Name who objects and answer in one line each.
Show what you trade away to get what you need.
How the bank makes the plan self-reinforcing.
One number with its time frame; the rest in a quiet row.
Who executes, plus the skeptics you brought along.
The vote you need, said once, loud.

templates.name: Romeo and Juliet: Why we should elope
templates.modelName: the Romeo and Juliet proposal structure
templates.hook: One secret wedding ends the feud. Every risk is low.
whatMakesItWork: The feud has a meter: A gauge swings from "ancient grudge" to "pure love" the moment the wedding happens. Projected, obviously.
The week plays itself: Sunday to Thursday, scene by scene, each one lighting up in order. Every card is true. None of them are reassuring.
A risk register you can check: Six risks, all rated Low. Click one to flip it and see the act and scene where it happens.
The advisor gets his own thesis back: The Friar's real motive, "turn your households' rancour to pure love", is the solution slide.

beats.job: Say the ask and the outcome in one sentence.
Make the stakes concrete: a count, a decree, a deadline.
Show the one move that changes the number, in the investor's own words.
Prove the moment: what changed in the last 24 hours.
Size it honestly, even when the answer is two people.
Count the signals you already have, however early.
Lay the milestones on a timeline the room can watch.
Name every risk before they do, with a mitigation each.
One line per person, and give the advisor a seat.
A term sheet: what, where, when, and the cover story.

templates.name: Willy Wonka: Golden Ticket launch
templates.hook: Five tickets. One factory. Zero leaks.
whatMakesItWork: You can tear open a bar: Click a wrapper and it rips. Usually it is chocolate. Once in a while it is a Golden Ticket, with the odds printed beside it.
The frenzy fills itself: Dots spread across a globe while five ticket slots fill in order, from Augustus to Charlie. Replay the hunt any time.
The tour is a route that counts down: The path draws room by room and "children remaining" drops from five to one as each guest finds their exit.
The twist is a job posting: The heir reveal arrives late, as an open role with four disqualifiers struck out one by one, followed by a risk register rated low across the board.

beats.job: The campaign in one line, with the hero object on screen.
The backstory as a story with villains, not a timeline.
The demand you already have: the question everyone keeps asking.
The campaign in one sentence, and let the room try it.
Top to bottom, with the scarcity made visible.
Show the buzz filling up, not a list of outlets.
Play the customer journey step by step.
Name the business outcome the campaign was built for.
List them plainly, with likelihood and a mitigation each.
One decision, one date.

templates.name: NASA: The moonshot budget
templates.hook: Nine billion dollars to win a race nobody else can see.
whatMakesItWork: The scoreboard fills in: Ten real firsts from Sputnik to Gagarin light up one by one. The score ends five all. The front pages end five to nothing.
Pick your option, see the odds: Toggle hold course, a lab in orbit, a robot on the Moon, or a crew on the Moon, and read the cost, the date and von Braun's own odds for each.
The budget draws itself: NASA by fiscal year, 1960 to 1966: year one adds $531 million, and by year four the agency is five times bigger.
The receipt itemizes the weather: Rover, communications and weather satellites each get a line. The Moon gets "the rest".

beats.job: The outcome and the deadline, in one line.
The one decision you need, and the first-year number, before any background.
Where you stand against the competition, counted honestly, with what the market notices marked.
The recent events that make waiting more expensive than acting, on a timeline.
Every real alternative, including doing nothing, with cost, timing and odds for each.
The option you chose and the one insight that makes it winnable.
Spend by year, so the approvers see year one and the peak.
What the money buys, itemized like a receipt, totals that match.
Gates with dates, and the slack against the deadline.
A register with an owner and a mitigation for each risk.
What counts as done, and what explicitly does not.
The numbers to approve, the commitment, and the return.

templates.name: Apollo 13: The incident review
templates.hook: Houston, we've had a post-mortem.
whatMakesItWork: Scrub the whole mission: 143 hours on one scrubber: drag from liftoff to splashdown and watch fourteen logged events light up, with the MET and the 1970 wall clock ticking alongside.
Five whys, one at a time: The board's findings become a five-whys chain that reveals cause by cause, from the bang at 55:54 back to a 1965 spec change nobody carried through.
The square peg, live: A CO2 gauge climbs toward the 7.5 mm Hg limit until the mailbox goes in. Flip the fix off and watch the needle run into the red.
Where we got lucky: The column most post-mortems skip: the lifeboat was still attached, the bad tank held for 56 hours, and Aquarius had 4.5 hours of power to spare.

beats.job: Incident name, detection time, severity, status, and the words "blameless review".
What happened, impact, root cause, resolution: four lines an executive can read in thirty seconds.
Lead with the outcome that matters most, then what it cost, in one hero number and a quiet row.
Every event with a timestamp, scrubbable, color-coded by phase.
Time to detect, diagnose and mitigate, plus every earlier signal you missed.
What the team did to stop the bleeding, in the order it happened.
The one fix that saved you, shown working against its limit.
Five whys, from the symptom to the decision that made it possible.
What went well, what went wrong, and where you got lucky, three items each.
Every fix with one owner and a type: prevent, detect, mitigate, process, learn.
Status, then dated follow-ups, so the review ends on what happens next.

templates.name: Jurassic Park: The board meeting after the storm
templates.modelName: the Jurassic Park board meeting structure (KPIs vs plan, incident, decisions)
templates.hook: Revenue: zero. Visitors: zero. Containment: below plan.
whatMakesItWork: Every KPI turns red on cue: Visitors, revenue, uptime, containment and NPS start on plan, then flip to red one row at a time. Containment: below plan.
The grid drops to zero: A control-room chart plays the weekend's power hour by hour, from 100% through the storm to zero. Scrub it yourself.
The board actually votes: Three motions with costs and a recommendation. Click approve or defer and the tally gets minuted.
Lowlights before highlights: Four lowlights, three highlights, in that order. The gift shop is fully stocked.

beats.job: The company, the meeting, the one-line truth, and the agenda. Send it as a pre-read.
The quarter in three lines: what happened, where we are, what we need.
Last meeting's priorities, each with its target and an honest red, yellow or green.
Every key metric against plan, with the variance and a status, bad ones included.
A neutral, timestamped summary of the quarter's defining event. Facts, no adjectives.
One operational chart, annotated with the events from the timeline.
Two or three causes, not symptoms, each with a concrete fix. Blame the system, not the person.
Bad news first and longer. It buys trust for the good news.
Revenue, burn by line, cash, and months of runway, stated plainly.
Two or three motions with cost and recommendation, for the board to approve or defer.
Three priorities with a target and one owner each. They become the next scorecard.
Questions, closed session, and the date of the next meeting. No thank-you slide.

templates.name: Apple: The iPhone launch keynote
templates.hook: Three products. One device. Zero buttons.
whatMakesItWork: Three icons spin into one: An iPod, a phone and a web tile orbit the stage, then land in the dock of a phone that wasn't there a second ago. Replay it as often as Steve repeated the list.
Plastic morphs into glass: A 2006 smartphone loses its keyboard on cue. Flip between Phone, Text and iPod: the plastic keys never change, the glass redraws itself for every app.
A demo phone you can unlock: Drag the slider, flick Cover Flow, search the map for coffee near Moscone West, and order 4,000 lattes before hanging up.
The goal is a sliver: A billion phones next to every other gadget market, with the 1% goal drawn in blue. Drag the share and watch 10 million grow.

beats.job: Open on one sentence, the place and the date. Nothing else on the slide.
Why today: the company's past breakthroughs on a timeline, and this one next.
One napkin chart of what is wrong with today's category.
Name the pieces, let the room solve it, then say the product's name.
The three jobs it does, each strong enough to be a product on its own.
The one technical idea, shown as a before and after.
Three or four live moments the audience will retell.
Name buyers by what they already carry and pay for.
Do the price math out loud, then dates, regions and partners.
One number you can be held to next year, against the market size.
A closing surprise bigger than the product, then get off stage.

templates.name: The Wright brothers: The December 1903 investor update
templates.modelName: the Wright brothers' investor update structure
templates.hook: Success. Four flights Thursday morning. Inform press.
whatMakesItWork: The telegram types itself: The TL;DR is the real telegram, typed out letter by letter, then corrected in red pencil: 57 becomes 59 and "Orevelle" becomes Orville.
The flight log replays: All four flights draw over the Kill Devil Hills sand in their real durations, sped up 30x. Click any flight to fly it again.
Burn, divided by flights: Under $1,000 against Langley's $70,000 of mostly public money. Flip to "per successful flight" and Langley's bar becomes a division by zero.
Lowlights with status pills: The wreck, John Daniels tumbling with it, the three-second stall: written as a candid ledger, the way GitLab's update template demands.

beats.job: Who it is from, who it is to, and the month in one line.
The whole update in the length of a telegram: outcome, headline number, ask, next date.
Two or three specific requests, each with an owner and a due date. Put them near the top.
One hero number with its time frame, then the same 4 to 6 KPIs as every month, each against plan or last period.
The trend behind the hero number, so investors see the slope, not just the point.
Two or three wins, each with evidence, including the work that made the result possible.
The misses, stated plainly, with a status for each. Never skip this section.
What you spent, where the money came from, and how long it lasts. Benchmark it.
Your position against the best-funded rival, row by row, with dates.
Next period's priorities with a target for each; they open next month's update.
Name the people who helped, then restate the one action you need.

templates.name: The 2002 Oakland A's: The Moneyball business case
templates.modelName: the Moneyball ROI business case structure
templates.hook: 103 wins at a third of the price.
whatMakesItWork: The ROI model has visible assumptions: Slide replacement-level wins and the roster floor, pick a rival, and watch the cost of a marginal win: $636K for Oakland, $2.20M for the Yankees.
All 30 clubs on one chart: Payroll against wins for every 2002 team. The league line says $40M buys 74 wins. Oakland sits 29 above it.
Baseball cards price the work: Flip between first base and the bullpen: Hatteberg got on base for $4,245 a time, Giambi for $34,762. Bradford recorded outs at $1,040 each.
The streak lights the scoreboard: Twenty lamps, twenty real scores, and game 20 told in three frames: 11-0, 11-11, Hatteberg.

beats.job: The result and the price on one line, before anything else.
The one approval you need today, with the unit economics that justify it.
What standing still costs, in the buyer's own currency.
Every real alternative, including doing nothing, with why it fails. One recommended.
What the market misprices, shown with like-for-like unit costs.
The formula, its assumptions as controls, and the result the buyer drives.
Your result plotted against every peer, with the trend line drawn.
The moment that made it undeniable, told as a sequence.
A register: what could go wrong, what you will do, and its status.
Past, now and next on one line, with where we are pinned.
The ask restated, one button, and the date it is needed by.

templates.name: Blockbuster: The Netflix meeting, take two
templates.hook: They passed on Netflix for $50M. This is the deck they needed next.
whatMakesItWork: The late fee has a price tag: Drag how much late-fee revenue to give up, pick a plan price, and watch a wall of VHS tapes fill to the 3.3 million subscribers it takes just to stand still.
The plan, years early: A timeline flips between what happened and the plan: the same moves slide back to 2000 and 2001, and red bars measure exactly how late each one came.
Tripwires that actually tripped: Netflix's first-ever subscriber decline, -55,000, gets a red TRIPPED stamp. Then the deck notes, deadpan, that Blockbuster pulled back anyway.
A VCR counter rewinds to 0001: From close to 7,700 stores through the 9,094 peak to one store in Bend, Oregon, on a glowing tape counter.

beats.job: Name the challenger and the exact line of your business it targets, with its size today drawn to scale.
Their customer journey next to yours; show the moment of yours that their pitch is built on.
The revenue line at risk as one poster number and its share of the total.
A calculator for the revenue you give up, what has to replace it, and what else you cannibalize.
Every real option, including doing nothing and buying them, with one marked as the pick.
The chosen response as an ordered list of moves, with the price of the first one.
When each move lands, set against the default path if you wait.
Three numbers with triggers, agreed in advance, that tell you it's working before the P&L does.
Where the core business goes if the room passes, in the most concrete unit you have.
One yes or no, the items it approves, and who signs.

templates.name: Spanx: Sara Blakely's fitting-room demo
templates.hook: Ten minutes and one ladies' room.
whatMakesItWork: Drag the before and after: One pair of cream pants, split down the seam: drag left for panty lines, right for smooth. The ladies' room, without the trip.
The agenda has a ladies' room: A ten-minute tape measure ticks through the meeting while the restroom door flips from Vacant to Occupied to Smooth.
Restock the beige wall: Eleven beige boxes and one red one. Shuffle the shelf as often as you like; you find the red one first every time.
It ends on a purchase order: Seven stores, $20 a pair, three weeks, with a dated action plan for both sides and an Approved stamp. Never "Thank you".

beats.job: The outcome in a few words, and the one object that proves it.
What the buyer's customers say, quoted the way the buyer hears it.
One slide of origin: the moment, the budget, the scrappy proof you mean it.
Let the buyer see the difference with their own eyes, ideally by dragging it.
The agenda for the part where you stop talking and show it.
Three promises and the price. Winners spend less time on features.
Show it in the buyer's world: their shelf, their screen, their workflow.
One story from someone like the buyer's customer saying yes.
The four questions they were about to ask, answered before they ask.
The path after yes, from the first order to the big outcome.
The exact next step, with dates and owners on both sides.

templates.name: Barbie: Ruth Handler's pitch to Mattel
templates.hook: The doll is the razor. The wardrobe is the blade.
whatMakesItWork: The objection flips over: Each memo from the room ("mothers will never buy it") turns over on its own to the answer, with the proof underneath.
The wardrobe fills up: Slide the outfits from 0 to 22, pick a price from $1 to $5, and watch the $3 doll shrink to a sliver of what she spends.
A behavior chart, not a hunch: Baby doll, paper doll, Lilli and ours, checked row by row. Only one column is complete, and only one signature is missing.
Fifty-two weeks, lit: The toy industry lights up seven weeks of the year; Mattel lights all 52, next to the $500,000 bet that paid for it.

beats.job: Name the product and its promise in one line, with the product drawn, not described.
The behavior you saw, in the customer's own words or play, before any product.
Separate the user, the buyer and the gatekeeper; make the user the hero.
Show the behavior already exists, in a chart that compares today's options.
The proof you went and got yourself: what you bought, tested or saw elsewhere.
Specs, price and what sells separately, set like a catalog page.
Say leadership's objection out loud before they do, then answer it with proof.
The channel you already own, and why it beats the industry default.
A live model of the first sale and the repeat sales, with the assumptions visible.
A production run, a price and a launch date, plus a forecast you'll be held to.

templates.name: The Eras Tour: The Eras Tour year in review
templates.hook: 149 shows. Every seat sold.
whatMakesItWork: The record race runs live: The gross counts up past Ed Sheeran and Elton John, flags each record as it falls, then flips to per show: $13.9 million a night against about $3 million.
Every city lights up in sequins: A sequin world map lights all 149 shows in order, Glendale to Vancouver; drag the slider to scrub the tour and watch the countries tick to 21.
String your own bracelet: Type a stat or tap a preset and the beads re-string themselves: 149 SHOWS, 10.1M FANS, $2.077B.
The Swift Quake, on paper: A seismograph draws Seattle 2023 against the 2011 Beast Quake at twice the swing, with a button to play it again.

beats.job: The year in one line and who it is for: the team that did it.
The single result everyone should repeat, with three quiet supporting numbers.
The result next to the plan, last year, or the previous best, in total and per unit.
The product as it ran, and what changed during the year.
Where the work landed, shown on a map or timeline you can scrub.
One standout moment, measured by someone outside the team.
The behavior you did not plan for, and the number that shows it spread.
Outside sources that noticed: one document as the hero, the rest as stubs.

beats.beat: What did not go to plan
beats.job: The misses, plainly, each with what followed.
One lesson as the hero with its evidence, two more in a quiet list.
The people who did it, by team and by name, and what they got.
Done, now, next on one line, so the year ends on the next step.

templates.name: Elle Woods: The Harvard Law admissions video
templates.hook: Not serious? Read the score report.
whatMakesItWork: The résumé unfolds: A pink tri-fold opens panel by panel on entry: monogram, 4.0, 179, president of Delta Nu. One button folds it back up.
179 counts up the curve: The score report climbs from 120 while a marker runs the distribution to the 99.9th percentile.
Why Harvard, with or without Warner: A fit matrix shows the personal reason, strikes it in crimson pen, and Harvard still wins. Put Warner back in with one click.
The objection gets overruled: The committee's "not serious" flips to the ruling and the evidence, and a pink gavel lands.

beats.job: One line: your name, your credential, and the trait they are buying.
Your hardest number at poster size, against the field it beat.
One story where you did the job before you had it: claim, evidence, result.
A fit matrix against the alternatives. Show your personal reason, then show you win without it.
The one skill nobody else in the cohort has, then the rest as a quiet list.
Name their doubt in their words and answer it with evidence, not adjectives.
The voucher who knows your work best, up front; the rest kept short.
The exact seat or role and the start date. Then stop.

templates.name: Mean Girls: Making fetch happen: a growth post-mortem
templates.hook: Three launches, one evangelist, zero repeats.
whatMakesItWork: Push harder, stay flat: Drag the "Push harder" slider and Gretchen's mentions climb toward a thousand while the line for everyone else never leaves zero.
Five whys, rung by rung: A ladder that walks from "nobody else said it" down to the root cause: a word with no pull, pushed through one person with a veto.
The cafeteria, as a network: Janis's lunch-table map becomes a spread chart: fetch lights one table, candy-cane grams light all of them.
Stop, keep, start, with owners: Stop fetch, keep pink Wednesdays, start pre-briefing the gatekeeper. Every decision has a name and a date.

beats.job: Name the bet that failed, plainly, and promise the reason.
The result first: one number that says how far off it was, with the supporting counts.
The bet, the hypothesis, and the success criteria as written before launch.
One chart of the metric that mattered against the one you were tempted to watch.
Every attempt in order, with what happened after each, and any outside benchmark.
Five whys from the symptom to a cause about systems and decisions, never a person.
Map where adoption happened and where it didn't, next to a channel that already reaches everyone.
Name what worked so it survives into the next attempt.
This time versus next time, one line each.
Stop, keep, start, each with one owner and one date.
The leading indicators, with thresholds, that would justify trying again.

templates.name: Mr. Darcy: The second proposal
templates.hook: The worst pitch in English literature, and the comeback.
whatMakesItWork: The first pitch gets a call review: Four of Darcy's own lines from Hunsford, each red-penned like a sales coach would ("Insults the buyer's family. Mid-pitch."), circled 0/4.
Every objection gets struck through: Her charges from chapter 34 strike out one by one, each replaced by what he actually did. Click a row to put the charge back.
The cost, in pounds and in pride: An account book straight from Mrs. Gardiner's letter: more than £2,000 counted up on one side; on the other, the total is Wickham as a brother-in-law.
April versus today, at the flick of a switch: The two proposals side by side, line for line, from "In vain have I struggled" to "one word from you will silence me on this subject for ever."

beats.job: Name what you are asking for again, with a line they will recognise.
The loss on record, with their reason in their own words.
Review your last pitch honestly. No excuses, no "but".
Play back each objection and sort it: misinformation to explain, fair points to fix.
Answer the misinformation with documents and a witness, fast.
Each objection beside the specific change that answers it.
Evidence they have seen for themselves, ideally unscripted, plus one reference.
The investment behind the change, in money and in pride. It proves the change is real.
Old pitch and new pitch side by side: same value, new terms.
One small decision in their hands, with what happens either way and an owner on each side.

templates.name: Cher Horowitz: The report card negotiation
templates.hook: Every grade is an opening offer.
whatMakesItWork: The report card renegotiates itself: Apply the heartbreak story, the tardy objection and the matchmaking, and watch the red pen go to work until the average lands on A-minus.
Positions flip to interests: Pick Miss Stoeger, Miss Geist or Mr. Hall and flip from what each one says to what each one actually wants, with the move that serves it.
Mr. Hall's mood is a slider: Drag him from miserable to in love and watch his ceiling climb past Cher's walk-away until the zone of agreement opens.
The closet computer picks the options: Cher's outfit computer scores every option by who it makes happy, and finds the one that makes everybody happy: a match.

beats.job: Name the deal and reframe where you start: their first number is an opening offer.
The current position in the other side's own numbers, and why it matters to you.
Your anchor, the outcome you expect, the worst deal you will sign, and your BATNA if there is no deal.
For each person across the table, the position they state and the interest underneath it.
Their limit against yours; if there is no overlap, show what would move their limit.
Options that cost you little and are worth a lot to them, scored by who each one helps.
Your opening ask and a ledger of planned concessions: what you give, and what you get for each.
The pushback you expect, each with a rehearsed answer, and where negotiation will not work.
Before and after, in their units, so everyone signs the same thing.
A mutual action plan: owners on both sides and a date for each step.

templates.name: Runway: The cerulean trend report
templates.hook: It was never just blue.
whatMakesItWork: Scrub it down the curve: Drag cerulean along Rogers' adoption curve from the runway to the clearance bin; the sweater rides the curve and the price tag marks itself down at every step.
A swatch book with math: Re-dye the sweater in real Pantone Colors of the Year and read the CIEDE2000 distance: Serenity (2016) is only 6 away. Cerulean came back.
The org chart that chose it: Six rooms, from the color council to the markdown desk, each with what it decided and the instrument it used. You report to all of them.
Theory, sourced: Veblen's imitation and Simmel's differentiation drawn as a staircase, so the "so what" lands: mass adoption is the top's exit signal.

beats.job: State the trend in one sentence anyone could repeat, with the exact thing being tracked.
Pin it down precisely against its nearest neighbors, so the team chases the right thing.
Date the first sightings and name the source for each.
Plot who adopted it, in order, on an adoption curve, with what changed at each step (price, channel, audience).
Map the gatekeepers who move it, and what each one actually controls.
Place it on the curve today and say what has replaced it at the leading edge.
Say which end of the curve you sell to, and what this stage means for that.
Stop, harvest, seed: each move with an owner, a date and a measure.
Leading signals in the order they fire, each tied to the action it triggers.
Close on the one call you need from the room.

templates.name: Taylor's Version: The re-recording business case
templates.hook: Can't buy it? Make it again.
whatMakesItWork: The calculator does the case: Drag the studio-cost and fan-switch assumptions and watch dollars per point of listening you own: building wins unless almost nobody switches. The real switch rate is pinned in pen.
Which version do you stream?: Toggle Taylor's Version against the originals across four albums: 20.5 billion US streams to 12.7 billion, with Fearless the one holdout.
The paperwork is the brand: Record sleeves, a studio track sheet, a work order with the box ticked in ballpoint, and an Approved stamp. No album art, just the stationery.
Both tracks finish: A tape-style timeline plays from November 2020: four re-records land on Track B, then Track A closes on May 30, 2025.

beats.job: One sentence: buy this, or build our own. What you are asking them to approve.
The dated events that forced the decision, and the window that just opened.
What you get, the price with its source, the terms on offer, and the timeline.
What you would make, what you would own, the cost basis, and the bonus only building gives you.
Weighted criteria agreed up front, scored side by side, including the row the other option wins.
A calculator with sourced figures and labeled assumptions, so the room can test the break-even.
A register for both options, each risk with a mitigation and an owner.
The pilot result, against the benchmark you set.
Whether users actually switched, shown as a share, with the exception called out.
The call, then the line items to approve and when you review it.
Both tracks on one timeline, with the milestone that closes each.

templates.name: Leonardo da Vinci: The letter to the Duke of Milan
templates.hook: Nine war machines. Also, painting.
whatMakesItWork: The capabilities are an engineering sheet: Click any of the ten items and its mechanism draws itself in sepia ink and red chalk. Item ten is an easel.
History reranks the services: Flip from the 1482 order to 2026 fame and watch painting climb from the last line of the letter to the top.
The flagship has a project tracker: Drag from the offer to the clay model, the bronze going to cannon, French archers, and the horse finally cast in 1999.
The ask is a demo slip: Pick the item you want proved and the request fills in: your park, or wherever your Excellency pleases.

beats.job: Name the studio and its promise in one line, with one signature piece of work.
Show that every rival offers the same thing, in the client's own terms.
Numbered capabilities the client can browse, each with a concrete example.
Credentials, real past work, and one reference, set as a list the client can check.
Four steps from brief to delivery, ending in something the client sees.
What else you do, and how it ranks, so the client can buy more later.
The one signature project, with its milestones laid out as a plan.
A demonstration on the client's terms: what, where, and when they choose.

templates.name: Tesla: The Secret Master Plan
templates.modelName: the Tesla Master Plan roadmap structure
templates.hook: Sports car first. It pays for the rest.
whatMakesItWork: The plan meets what shipped: A Now, Next, Later board with confidence by horizon. Toggle it and the real ship dates stamp on: Feb 2008, June 2012, July 2017.
The money actually flows: Cash runs from the Roadster to the family car to the third car. Flip to "cheap car first" and the pipe runs dry at step one.
One roadmap, two audiences: Internal shows confidence, dates and dependencies. Customer hides them all and leaves four lines and "Don't tell anyone."
Outcomes, not cars: Success is measured in grams of CO2 per kilometre, with the post's own well-to-wheel numbers drawn as the chart.

beats.job: The outcome the roadmap serves, as a from-and-to. Products are outputs.
A timeline of what has happened, with a "you are here" pin and the next real milestone.
The whole roadmap on one board, each horizon with its confidence level.
What is committed and funded, with the specs that prove it is real.
What is planned, as a direction and a target, no date until there is one.
A direction only, deliberately vague, plus any parallel track.

beats.beat: How each step unlocks the next
beats.job: Dependencies as a flow, with the alternative that breaks it.
The obvious options you rejected, each with its reason.
The outcome metric that says the plan is working, with a baseline.
The same roadmap with confidence, dates and dependencies hidden for customers.
End on the date of the next roadmap, never "Thank you".

templates.name: Ben & Jerry's: The gas station business plan
templates.hook: Two friends, a $5 course, and an old gas station.
whatMakesItWork: The ledger adds itself up: Sources and uses of the $12,000 write themselves in, the running total ticks to the bank's third, and the $5 course gets its own line.
Break-even you can argue with: Drag the cone price, July traffic and monthly costs; twelve months of bars show exactly how much summer has to carry the winter.
The corner, on a map: Our own drawing of downtown Burlington: tap the shop, the campus up the hill, Church Street, the park across the road and the lake.
Chunks, adjustable: A chunk-size slider runs from supermarket flecks to ours, because the co-founder doing quality control tastes in texture.

beats.job: What you sell and where, in one sentence on the cover.
Who buys, and what they can't get today, shown as the reason for this place.
What makes it different, shown rather than listed.
Where the customers are, drawn on a map with the site pinned.
The real alternatives, including doing nothing, with the biggest one as the hero.
The channels, cheapest first, with one clear lead.
How the product is made and delivered, day to day.
Why these people can run it: credentials first, one playful detail.
Sources and uses of funds, and how much the owners put in.
The break-even point and first-year months, with every assumption labeled.
A register with likelihood and a mitigation for each, biggest first.
The amount, what it buys, the dated milestones, and how it gets repaid.

templates.name: Mr. Miyagi: Wax on, wax off
templates.hook: Four days of chores. Every one a block.
whatMakesItWork: The chores flip into blocks: Four cards (sponge, sandpaper, fence brush, house brush) turn over one by one into the block each one trained. Click to flip them back.
The deck quizzes you: A no-notes check with three questions and instant feedback, because tested students remembered 56% a week later and re-readers 42%.
The practice log ties the belt: Two weeks of spaced practice, each chore returning a little later each time; log the days and a gi belt fills to the knot.
Outcomes, not topics: "Block a punch without thinking about it", with how it gets checked. Karate history and belt theory are struck off the syllabus.

beats.job: Name the learner, the program and the first thing to bring.
Up to four things they will be able to do, each with how it gets checked.
The stakes in writing: what changes if they learn this, and what happens if they don't.
One skill, practiced on the slide, before the theory.
A no-notes quiz with instant feedback. Retrieval beats re-reading.
What builds on the first one, one new piece at a time.
Now name what they have been practicing and why it works.
A calendar where each skill returns after growing gaps, with unannounced checks.
Where it gets used for real, under pressure, with nobody prompting.
Who is in their corner, starting with an active manager.
Exactly what to do first, and when the first check-in is booked.

templates.name: Coca-Cola: The Pepsi Challenge and New Coke
templates.modelName: the New Coke competitive analysis structure
templates.hook: 200,000 sips said change it. The can disagreed.
whatMakesItWork: Take the blind test: Pick cup M or cup Q on the one-sip promise, then see the reveal: you just voted like 191,000 tasters in Project Kansas.
Sip versus can: Behind a one-way mirror, toggle one sip, half a can, and a whole can, and watch the winner change from the sweeter formula to the one people grew up with.
The SWOT with an empty box: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats are all full. The fifth box, what customers feel, says "Not measured" until you press "What we missed".
The test plays out: The recommendation says "watch the hotline"; then the hotline counts from 400 to 1,500 calls a day and the timeline runs 79 days to Classic.

beats.job: The finding and the matchup in one line: who is winning what.
The one question this analysis answers, and the decision riding on it.
Share over time for you and the main rival, with the gap you are trying to explain.
A grid of the dimensions that matter, with the one row you lose highlighted.
What buyers say they want, and exactly how you measured it: sample, cost, format.
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, plus a box for what customers feel, so it leads to a move.

beats.beat: What the data can't tell us
beats.job: The limits of the method: what it measured versus how people actually buy and use.
Three things that must now be true, and the stake if you act on them.
The move, the date, and the signals with baselines that would prove you wrong.
The lesson to carry into the next analysis, stated as a rule.

templates.name: The Kids, Inc.: Why we need a dog
templates.modelName: the party-pitch structure (serious format, personal stakes, a vote at the end)
templates.hook: A Series A for one good dog.
whatMakesItWork: The budget always wins: Drag food, vet and toys as high as you like. The dog lands under therapy every time, because Leo's allowance quietly absorbs the rest.
The chore chart checks itself: Thirty-five boxes fill in day by day as the slide opens, and the room can tap any of them. The promise is the visual.
Investor costume, all the way down: Traction is hours walking the neighbor's dog, the market is a house score docked six points for the white rug, and each sibling signs an SLA.
The vote happens in the room: The last slide is a live ballot with two options, Yes and Absolutely, a running tally, and confetti on every vote.

beats.job: Put a personal ask in a corporate costume: "Series A, for Mom and Dad".
One concrete, slightly tragic artifact (a greeting log of zeros).
The thing you want, labeled like a product spec.
Proof you already do the work, as a chart that goes up and to the right.
A chore chart with owners, so the objection is answered before it is raised.
Score your readiness and own the one weakness out loud.
Compare the cost to something absurdly worse, and let them play with it.
Each person, a title, and a promise they can be held to.
A 2x2 where the alternatives lose with a joke each.
Quote every likely no and answer it in one line.
One thing, one condition, one date, on a term sheet.
Decide in the room, with options that all mean yes.
